content: Holiday heart syndrome is a clinical condition characterized by an irregular heartbeat in individuals who are otherwise healthy. It is often triggered by stress, dehydration, and alcohol consumption, with excessive alcohol intake being the most common cause. While it is typically associated with binge drinking, it can also occur in individuals who are not heavy drinkers. The underlying pathophysiology of holiday heart syndrome, also referred to as alcohol-induced arrhythmia, is complex and not fully understood. Chronic consumption of large amounts of ethanol is believed to lead to structural and cellular changes in the heart due to the accumulation of ethanol and its metabolites. The incidence and prevalence of holiday heart syndrome remain unclear due to conflicting evidence. If left untreated, it can progress to severe cardiomyopathy, valvular disease, and even death. Some patients may also develop end-stage liver disease, which carries a poor prognosis. However, if diagnosed early and managed with measures such as alcohol cessation, the prognosis is favorable, as the condition is reversible. Patients with acute alcohol exposure may present with a variety of symptoms. Holiday heart syndrome is also known as alcohol-induced atrial fibrillation. On physical examination, patients often exhibit signs of alcohol intoxication, including the smell of alcohol on their breath. Mental status changes may be observed due to intoxication, and some patients may be hypotensive. Depending on the cardiac rhythm, the pulse may be irregular or thready. A complete blood count may reveal macrocytic anemia with an elevated mean corpuscular volume. Elevated white blood cell counts may also be seen, as alcoholics often have reduced immunity and are more prone to infections. A complete metabolic panel may show a 2:1 ratio of aspartate aminotransferase (AST) to alanine aminotransferase (ALT), indicative of alcoholic liver disease. Twelve-lead electrocardiography (ECG) is essential to rule out other cardiac pathologies such as ischemia, infarction, pulmonary embolism, or hypertrophy. A chest X-ray may reveal cardiomegaly, and an echocardiogram should be performed to assess for structural abnormalities, cardiac function, and chamber enlargement. The treatment of holiday heart syndrome depends on the patient’s vital signs at presentation. For unstable patients with atrial fibrillation, cardioversion is the recommended treatment. Stable patients are typically managed with medications to address arrhythmias. Complete cessation of alcohol is necessary to reverse the disease process. Patients should be encouraged to join support groups such as Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) to maintain abstinence. The pathophysiology of holiday heart syndrome involves both direct and indirect effects of alcohol on the myocardium. Chronic ethanol consumption can lead to oxidative stress in the heart by increasing free radical production and activating the renin-angiotensin system. Ethanol metabolites, particularly acetaldehyde, cause oxidative damage, mitochondrial dysfunction, and cell death, leading to myocyte loss and adverse cardiac remodeling. Altered fatty acid metabolism and increased catecholamine levels also contribute to arrhythmias. The most common arrhythmia observed in holiday heart syndrome is atrial fibrillation, followed by atrial flutter and premature ventricular contractions. The primary cause of holiday heart syndrome is excessive alcohol consumption, often exacerbated by binge drinking episodes. Other contributing factors include excessive caffeine intake, overeating, fatigue, stress, and dehydration. Holiday heart syndrome must be differentiated from other conditions such as alcoholism, arrhythmias (e.g., paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter), cirrhotic cardiomyopathy, dilated cardiomyopathy, psychiatric disorders, hyperthyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, and pulmonary embolism. The natural history of untreated holiday heart syndrome can lead to severe complications, including worsening heart failure, life-threatening arrhythmias, thromboembolism, and death. Early diagnosis and alcohol cessation improve the prognosis, as the condition is reversible. Symptoms of holiday heart syndrome include dizziness, exertional dyspnea, chest pain, unconsciousness, and heart palpitations. Palpitations are the most common presenting symptom and may be intermittent or persistent, depending on the presence of sustained arrhythmias and the ventricular response to atrial fibrillation. Other symptoms include fatigue, weakness, angina, and signs of alcohol intoxication. Less common symptoms include swollen legs, nausea, and anxiety. On physical examination, patients may exhibit signs of alcohol intoxication, including a strong odor of alcohol on their breath. Cardiac findings may include an irregularly irregular pulse, protodiastolic (S3) and presystolic (S4) heart sounds, and hypotension. Advanced cases may show signs of right heart failure, such as jugular venous distention, ascites, and peripheral edema. Laboratory findings in holiday heart syndrome may include macrocytosis, thrombocytopenia, elevated white blood cell counts, and a 2:1 AST to ALT ratio suggestive of alcoholic liver disease. Serum levels of gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase may also be elevated. Magnesium and thiamine levels are often low in alcoholics. Biomarkers such as ethyl glucuronide and ethyl sulfate in urine, as well as phosphatidylethanol (PEth) in blood, can indicate recent alcohol consumption. Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin is useful for identifying relapse after a period of abstinence. ECG findings may include arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, QT interval prolongation, increased QRS duration, and conduction abnormalities like left bundle branch block. A chest X-ray may show cardiomegaly, and echocardiography is the standard of care for assessing cardiac chamber enlargement, left ventricular wall motion abnormalities, hypertrophy, valvular disease, and systolic and diastolic dysfunction. Liver ultrasound may reveal cirrhosis, as liver disease is often associated with holiday heart syndrome. Treatment typically involves rest, hydration, and cessation of alcohol intake. Symptoms such as atrial fibrillation and conduction abnormalities often resolve within 6 to 12 hours with these measures. For patients presenting with atrial fibrillation, intravenous hydration and medications to control heart rate may be administered. Unstable patients may require cardioversion. Long-term management includes complete alcohol cessation and participation in support groups. Prevention of holiday heart syndrome involves abstinence from alcohol, electrolyte replacement, adequate hydration, and stress management. Limiting salt and sugar intake can help control blood pressure, and maintaining a healthy lifestyle can reduce the risk of recurrence.
